The heathens said: *"Eigi er undr í, at goðin reiðist tölum slíkum"* — no wonder the gods are angry at talk like this.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun
en: **Then Snorri goði.** *"Um hvat reiddust goðin, þá er hér brann hraunit, er nú stöndum vér á?"* — **"What were the gods angry about when the lava we are now standing on burned?"** And note exactly where he was pointing: **at the ground under his own feet, at Þingvellir.** Not at this field. He was telling the pagans that their own holy assembly ground was made of the same stuff, laid down by the same fire, long before anyone was around to be blamed for it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun

But it ran **north-east, into Þrengslin** — nowhere near the farm everybody was panicking about. Vísindavefur puts it plainly: it seems unlikely the flow ever actually threatened Þóroddur's farm. **The most famous omen in Icelandic history was, on the best reading of the map, a false alarm.**

ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: A field of perfect little volcanoes, and **not one of them is real**. We dug half of them up for road gravel — and that turned out to be the reason NASA got interested.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: **They are fake volcanoes.** *Gervigígar* — properly, **rootless cones**. No conduit, no magma chamber underneath, no roots at all. The magma did not come up; it came **sideways**, through closed lava tubes just under the surface.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: **What actually happened:** lava from the shield crater **Leiti**, in the eastern **Bláfjöll** ridge, ran about **28 km** all the way down to **Elliðaárvogur** — so fluid that in places the flow is only **0.6 to 0.75 m thick.** Where it crossed wet ground, its own base crust held the water off until the weight cracked it. Water-saturated sediment then met molten lava, and the result was not a polite puff of steam but **repeated explosive mixing** — fragmentation, ash fall, ballistic ejecta — punching **back up through the flow.** Frozen mid-explosion in red scoria. The red is iron oxide. It is rust.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: **How old? Genuinely disputed, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.** **Náttúrufræðistofnun Íslands** says **5,200 years**. A University of Iceland thesis says **5,316**. **Vísindavefur** says **4,700**. **Reykjavíkurborg** says **4,500** for the same lava down in Elliðaárdalur. Four institutions, four numbers, one lava. Somewhere between four and a half and five and a half thousand years old.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: **How many cones?** The only hard count anybody ever made is **von Komorowicz's map of 1912**, which numbers **98 craters** — cone 53 was one of the biggest — plus **hornitos** on the eastern side that **are not there any more.** He thought they were real scoria cones; nobody had worked out the mechanism yet. Today the field covers about **0.8 km²** and only a handful of intact cones survive, round the edges.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: **Because we quarried the rest.** Rauðhólar was largely untouched until about **1940**, when the British occupation brought heavier machinery than this country had ever had and a war's appetite for aggregate. Red scoria made excellent road surfacing and you could shovel it **straight onto a lorry bed**. The single biggest job it fed was **building Reykjavík Airport in Vatnsmýri**. Digging ran hardest from **1940 to 1950**, and was still going in **1949** — into Hringbraut — the year the geologist **Sigurður Þórarinsson** stood up at the Natural History Society's 60th anniversary and said out loud that we were destroying it. An aerial photograph from **28 July 1954** shows how much was already gone.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: **It was then protected twice.** As a **náttúruvætti — a natural monument — in 1961**, and again as a **fólkvangur in 1974** (*Auglýsing um fólkvang í Rauðhólum* nr. **185/1974**). Every pseudocrater in Iceland now carries special protection under **náttúruverndarlög nr. 60/2013**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: **Now the Mars part, which is real, and which is not the story people tell.** Nobody trained astronauts here. What happened is that when Mars images began arriving from about **1970**, the crater clusters on them looked exactly like these — same shape, same formation conditions, same volcanism. So between **2002 and 2016**, fieldwork here funded by **NASA's Mars Data Analysis Program, Mars Fundamental Research Program and NASA Postdoctoral Program** used the **quarry faces** — the damage — to work out how a rootless cone is built on the inside, and applied it to the Red Planet. **The vandalism is the reason the science was possible.** There is nowhere else in Iceland you can look inside one of these.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: For scale, Iceland's big pseudocrater fields are **Landbrotshólar at 150 km²**, **Álftavershólar at 35**, **Mývatn at 30** and **Aðaldalur at 28**. Rauðhólar is **0.8**. It is the small one. It is also the one twenty minutes from a capital city, which is exactly why it went under a runway.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: The shallow lake beside them is **Rauðavatn**, "Red Water", and that scruffy belt of trees is the **oldest deliberate woodland in the Reykjavík area.** In **1901** about eighty shareholders founded **Skógræktarfélag Reykjavíkur**, bought **six hectares** by the lake and put the Danish forester **C. E. Flensborg** in charge of the summers. They dug **8,600 holes in 1902** and planted about **8,000 rowan** the next summer. Frost killed nearly all of it, and the fence never held — a newspaper in **1918** grumbled that the livestock *gengur þar inn og út*, in and out as they pleased. Only after the Second World War, with close to **60,000 plants**, did it finally take. The oldest mountain pines by the lake are now **over a hundred years old.** (How do you find your way out of an Icelandic forest? Stand up. This is where somebody first set out to ruin that joke, and they have been at it for a hundred and twenty-four years.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: **Ari the Wise** wrote in *Íslendingabók* that at settlement Iceland was *viði vaxið milli fjalls og fjöru* — wooded from the mountains to the shore. Today woodland covers about **1.5%** of the country.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: Behind the cones lies **Elliðavatn**, and on a low spit in it, **Þingnes**: **16–17 surface ruins, at least 18 structures**, and two nested circles nobody has ever pinned a function on. The state registers it as *hinn forni Kjalarnessþingstaður*, the ancient Kjalarnes assembly place — **signed 25 October 1930, entered 16 November 1938.** Whether it really is the þing **Ari fróði** put on **Kjalarnes**, fourteen kilometres that way, has never been proven by anybody.

en: It looks like a Sunday-stroll park. It's a five-thousand-year-old construction site nobody ever closed.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur
en: To joggers it's a postcard. To a geologist, it's a **crime scene** — ten thousand years of Iceland trying, and failing, to stay quiet.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur
en: The whole valley was redesigned when **Leiti** erupted. The crater is **Leitin**, east of **Bláfjöll**, the lava is **Leitahraun**, and it is a textbook **helluhraun** — the smooth, ropy kind you can walk on. It poured down here, hit the river and **split it in two**. Before, one river. After, two.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur
en: How long ago? Somebody dug the answer out of this valley: a radiocarbon date on **birch charcoal found underneath the lava, right here in Elliðaárdalur**, gives **about 4,600 years**. Other estimates for the same lava run up to about 5,300 — the same spread of dates that the **Rauðhólar** craters have, and for a very good reason. **Rauðhólar sit in this lava.** Same eruption, different souvenir.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur
en: Every waterfall in the valley is the river's four-and-a-half-thousand-year project to saw back down through that basalt to the sea. It is not finished.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur
en: The **Elliðaá** is one of very few **capital-city rivers anywhere with a wild Atlantic salmon run** — and there is a camera counter in it, so this is a counted number, not a boast. **1,533 fish in 2009**; **1,067 in 2003**. If you have heard "two and a half thousand salmon", that number is real but it is the wrong animal: **2,500 is a batch of smolts**, not returning adults.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur
en: Reykjavík was so taken with the river it **bought the whole thing in 1906**. Your city buys parks. We bought a river. The power station, **Elliðaárstöð, was switched on on 27 June 1921** and is still down there humming.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur
en: One kilometre of this valley has hosted a **1750s wool mill**, a **drowning pool at Skötufoss** for women convicted of "moral crimes", outlaws living in the lava tubes, **British WWII Quonset huts**, and a century-old hydro plant. And most Icelandically of all, a **burst pipe in 1998** flooded the place and washed **ten thousand years of buried history back into daylight in a single weekend.** Even the plumbing does archaeology here.

en: Weather pivot: "Weather barely touches this river. It drains a highland catchment, so it runs much the same in sun or sleet."

ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: Up ahead we cross **Iceland's longest river** — a **230 km** glacial spine that the settlers argued beside and engineers turned into the country's biggest battery.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: **Þjórsá** runs **230 km** to the sea, **Iceland's longest river**, draining a **7,530 km²** catchment. And it does not start where almost everyone says it does: it begins up in **Þjórsárdrög on northern Sprengisandur**, where the headstream carries the lovely name **Bergvatnskvísl**. The Hofsjökull line you will hear is a muddle — Hofsjökull and Vatnajökull feed the *catchment* that the power stations run on, which is not the same as the river's source.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: By the time it reaches **Urriðafoss**, just below the bridge, it is moving about **360 cubic metres a second**. Not a river you paddle absent-mindedly.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: **Urriðafoss** is **Iceland's most voluminous waterfall** — *vatnsmesti foss*, the one with the greatest average flow. It is not the tallest and it is not the most powerful; **Dettifoss** up north is the *aflmesti*, the most powerful. The two get swapped so reliably that the University of Iceland has had to correct it in print. Low, wide and unphotogenic beats tall and famous, if the metric is water.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: Every winter the river builds an ice jam here with its own name, the **Urriðafosshrönn** — ice and slush packing in until Iceland's most voluminous waterfall is simply not visible, buried under its own river. Landsvirkjun surveyed it in the winter of 2002–03; the numbers are in their report and not in my mouth.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: It does more electrical work than any river in Iceland. The classic cascade on the **Þjórsá–Tungnaá** system is **six stations** — Búrfell, Sultartangi, Hrauneyjafoss, Vatnsfell, Sigalda and Búðarháls, the last of those only since **2014**. Landsvirkjun now counts **seven**, because Búrfell got a second station, and the proposed **Hvammur** would be the eighth. The original **Búrfell came online on 16 September 1969**, and the reason a country of 380,000 people generates this much electricity is spelled **aluminium**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: People have wanted **Urriðafoss** itself since **1927**, when the poet **Einar Benediktsson's** company **Titan** was granted permission for a **160,000-horsepower** station here and never turned a sod. The modern version is **Urriðafossvirkjun** — **140 MW**, about **1,037 GWh a year** — and on **17 February 2026** Alþingi left it in **biðflokkur**, the hold category, with the committee specifically recommending against moving it to the use category. A hundred years of wanting, and the river is still winning on points.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: Midstream sits the island of **Árnes**, and the district is still called **Árnessýsla** after an assembly nobody can now locate. Alþingi's own research material says the scholars are split: **no assembly booths have ever been identified on the island**, while **thirty to forty** booth-like structures are recorded at **Búði**, on the north bank, where a spring assembly serving **three goðorð** ran until **963**. A whole county named after a meeting, and we have lost the room.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: About the name. **Landnámabók** says the settler **Þórarinn Þorkelsson** sailed into the mouth with a **bull's head on his prow**, giving *Þjórsá*, the bull river — **Árnastofnun** records the traditional reading as **Bolafljót**. But **Þórhallur Vilmundarson** argued the original was ***Þjótsá***, from the verb for roaring, pointing at the farm on the bank still called **Þjótandi**, "the one that roars". A river named either for a cow's head or for the noise it makes. Iceland has never settled it.

en: Carved into the soft sandstone beside the **Ytri-Rangá** is a cluster of **man-made caves**, some with simple **crosses** and **stone benches** cut into the wall.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🕳️ Hella
en: A popular theory ties them to the **Papar** — the Irish monks that **Íslendingabók** and **Landnámabók** both say were in Iceland *before* the Norse, and who left the moment longships appeared. Tempting. But honestly: the dating is **disputed**, and **no archaeology has confirmed a pre-Norse origin** for these caves. Treat it as suggestive, not settled. The caves are real, the crosses are real, the monks are a maybe.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🕳️ Hella
en: The town itself is a newcomer by comparison. **Hella dates from 1927**, when a trader who had been working out of **Rauðalækur** bought a small plot out of the land of the farm **Helluvað**, right by the bridge over the Ytri-Rangá, and opened a general store — and a slaughterhouse. Nothing anchors a settlement like being able to buy your groceries and butcher your lamb in one stop.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏡 Keldur
en: It was a seat of the **Oddaverjar**, the clan the sagas call the **"Kings of the South"**, and it stands square in **Njáls saga** country — its first inhabitant, **Ingjaldur Höskuldsson**, is named in the saga itself.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏡 Keldur

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏡 Keldur
en: And then the good bit. It is not romantic and it is not a secret passage for lovers. It is an **escape route**, in case somebody came in the night to **burn the house down with everyone asleep inside**. In this neighbourhood that was not paranoia. Ask Njáll.

en: A normal-looking service town that comes with its own **blood-soaked medieval bestseller** — and a field where people have actually dug for the ending.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur / 🏘️ Hvolsvöllur
en: **Hvolsvöllur** is the last full-service fuel stop before Vík, planted in the heart of **Brennu-Njáls saga** country — Iceland's **longest, bloodiest, most carefully built** family saga. The farms and low hills around you are its stage.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur / 🏘️ Hvolsvöllur
en: Written **late in the 1200s** but set around **the year 1000**, its set-piece is the **brenna** — the burning of **Njáll**, his wife **Bergþóra** and their sons at **Bergþórshvoll**, on the flat land just east of here, which the saga's own chronology puts around **1011**. *Game of Thrones*, except half the cast also had to be home for the haymaking.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur / 🏘️ Hvolsvöllur
en: And here is the part that makes it more than a story. **People went and dug it up.** **Sigurður Vigfússon** excavated Bergþórshvoll in **1883 and 1885**; the national antiquarian **Matthías Þórðarson** went back in **1927**, again in **1931**, and the work ran on to **1951** — seventy years of Icelanders looking for one fire. **They did find a burnt layer**, right at the bottom of the occupation deposits, from buildings that had plainly burned, its edges curled up against the walls. What nobody has ever been able to say is that it was **his** fire.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur / 🏘️ Hvolsvöllur
en: Odder still: **Bergþórshvoll is not in Landnámabók at all** — it was not a settlement farm. But Landnáma **twice mentions Njáll's burning as something everybody already knew about.** The event outran the address.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: In **1973** a brand-new volcano opened at the edge of a working fishing town — and the town **fought it with a fire hose and a dredger, and ended up with a better harbour than it started with.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: **Just before two in the morning on 23 January 1973**, a fissure tore open on the eastern side of **Heimaey**. Icelandic accounts give it as **1,600 metres with 30 to 40 vents**; the **USGS** says it opened to about **two kilometres, right across the island from shore to shore**, with submarine activity at both ends. Out of it came a volcano that had not existed the day before: **Eldfell**, "Fire Mountain", which grew to roughly the height of **Helgafell** standing next to it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: **The town was 5,273 people** — that is the census count of **1 December 1972**, seven weeks earlier. **Nearly all of them were off the island and safely on the mainland within six hours.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: **The reason it worked is that the fishing fleet was in port.** Iceland has **no army**; the evacuation was run by the people who happened to own boats. The explanation everybody gives — **including me** — is that a storm the day before had kept the fleet in. Be straight about it: **the fleet being in port is documented; the storm is the story that goes with it.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: **It did not stop for five and a half months.** The eruption **was not declared over until 3 July 1973.** For the whole of that spring Heimaey was a disaster zone, a building site and an active volcano at the same time, and people went to work in it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: **The damage, counted by early May:** about **300 buildings engulfed by lava or gutted by fire**, and another **60 to 70 homes buried completely by tephra**. Iceland's own Pompeii — and some of those houses have since been **dug back out** and left open at the **Eldheimar** museum.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: **Then the part nobody believes.** On **6 February** the **Vestmannaeyjar fire brigade** started spraying seawater at the lava front with hoses — about **100 litres a second**, which against a lava flow is a rounding error. On **1 March** the dredger **Sandey** arrived with **56-centimetre steel pipe** and pushed about **400 litres a second**. American equipment landed on **26 March**. By the time the pumps stopped on **10 July** they had put roughly **eight million cubic yards of North Atlantic seawater** onto the flow, through **43 pumps** and **more than nineteen miles — thirty kilometres — of pipe, three-quarters of it plastic.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: **And it worked.** The tongue of lava that had almost closed the harbour entrance **stopped where they cooled it**, and the USGS is blunt about what happened next: it **is now acting as a breakwater, protecting the harbour from storms.** The volcano tried to shut the port. The port came out **better sheltered than before.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: The lava and tephra also added **nearly a square mile** of new ground — **about 20% more island** than they started with.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: **On the deaths, be straight, because it is genuinely contested.** **Icelandic institutional sources record no deaths from the eruption.** **The USGS records one fatality — a man overcome by gas inside a building** — with several others partially affected. Those two accounts have **never been reconciled**, and I am not going to reconcile them for you out of a bus window. What I will say is that **the lurid version some guides tell, a looter overcome in a pharmacy basement, is not documented in any source I would stand behind.** A town of **5,273** got out from under an erupting fissure with, at the very most, one death. **That is the fact. It does not need decorating.**

en: The **Markarfljót** in front of you rises under **Torfajökull**, up in the highlands — not off the two ice caps everyone assumes. *Heima er bezt* puts it at about **75 km** from source to sea. Then again, ask how long it is and you have picked a fight: it is a **braided** river, and Iceland's national map data carries **190 separate channels** all called Markarfljót, adding up to well over 200 km of water. ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi
en: What **Eyjafjallajökull** and **Mýrdalsjökull** do is feed it lower down — two ice caps sitting on live volcanoes — which is why it occasionally stops being a river and becomes a **jökulhlaup**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi
en: **2010, and the bit everybody gets wrong.** You will hear that engineers deliberately cut the Ring Road embankment to save the bridge. What *Morgunblaðið* reported at the time is better: **the swollen river broke its own gap** in the flood dyke east of Markarfljót, and that is what took the load off the bridge. The deliberate version is a real Icelandic technique — at **Skeiðará in 1996** they cut **five gaps** in the embankment and planned to cut the road itself in two places — but here, the river did its own engineering and the engineers let it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌊 Landeyjar Plains
en: It looks like "just flat fields", but you are crossing a giant **flood-deposit fan**, built grain by grain by glacial rivers charging out of the highlands — chiefly the **Markarfljót**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌊 Landeyjar Plains
en: The name gives it away. **Landeyjar means "land islands"** — the grassy patches that stood up out of the marsh and sand back when the water still owned everything around them. Waves once rolled over where this road runs, and the sea came right up to that **cliff line** inland. Then the land rose, the rivers kept dumping sand, and the coastline **marched south, kilometre by kilometre**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌊 Landeyjar Plains
en: So the cliffs you can see used to be beach, and the beach is now several kilometres further out. Iceland does not have a coastline so much as a rolling negotiation.

en: This "empty" plain is also **Njáls saga's stage**. **Bergþórshvoll** — where Njáll and his family were burned alive, around **1011** in the saga's own reckoning — sits out here among the hayfields. en: A farmer here was digging ash out of his drinking water while airline chief executives were melting down 2,000 km away.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
en: It does not look like much: a tidy white lid over green fields. **Veðurstofa Íslands** describes what is actually under there — a cone **about 1,666 metres** high, the volcano itself **25 km long and 15 km wide**, mostly buried in ice, with a **crater about 2.5 km across**. It has been a fairly active volcano for the last **8,000 years**, and its magma runs **all the way from basalt to rhyolite** — which is exactly why it can produce fine, glassy ash instead of tidy lava.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
en: By volcanic standards **2010 was small**: a **VEI 4**, only about **0.27 km³** of ash. But it fired a **plume 8–9 km high** straight into the **jet stream**, and those glassy particles turn jet engines into **expensive sandblasters**. A small volcano in exactly the wrong place, pointing at exactly the wrong wind.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
en: The result was the **worst aviation shutdown in Europe since the Second World War** — **104,000 flights cancelled over eight days, 15 to 22 April**, about **48% of expected European traffic**, roughly **10 million passengers** who simply could not fly, and the airspace of some **20 countries** closed. Europe discovered that volcanoes do not read timetables.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
en: The first hit, though, was local. As meltwater poured off the ice, **500 to 800 people were evacuated overnight** from the farms below, and the ash fell thick enough to turn day into night. At **Þorvaldseyri**, right at the foot, they **milked the cows in respirator masks** and scraped ash off the roofs — and then built a visitor centre, because if a volcano is going to rewrite your year you may as well sell the story back.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
en: And the question every single group asks: **did it set off Katla next door?** Here is the honest answer. The two sit **25 km apart**. Eyjafjallajökull erupted in **1821–1823**, in **1612–1613** and **probably in 920**, and you will very often hear that Katla followed each time — but **Veðurstofa's own page lists those eruptions and does not make that claim**. What is certain is that in **2010 Katla stayed shut**. Treat this mountain as a warning light, not a trigger.

en: **Drangurinn** stands alone in the field like a stubborn leftover: a block of **móberg**, palagonite tuff, the same subglacial-eruption rock that built **Pétursey** further along this coast, left standing when the softer cliff around it weathered away. It is about **300 metres from the farmhouse**, in the home field of **Drangshlíð**, under the **Eyjafjöll** cliffs — which is why it looks dropped there rather than grown there.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🪨 Drangurinn
en: The saga version is more fun. **Grettir the Strong**, Iceland's great troublemaking outlaw, is said to have torn it out of the cliff above and thrown it down here, leaving a notch in the ridge behind. Once you have heard that, the notch stops looking like erosion and starts looking like a **missing tooth**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🪨 Drangurinn
en: Locals did not waste a rock this size. They **built turf barns and cowsheds straight up against it**, and the folklore — **Jón Árnason's** collection — says **elves live inside**, that they quietly mind the farmers' cows, and that at calving time they will even **milk them**. The most useful neighbours in Iceland, if you believe it, and rent-free stabling if you do not.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🪨 Drangurinn
en: Here is the part that should make the coach laugh: **people have been stopping for this rock for a century.** *Lesbók Morgunblaðsins*, in **1928**, wrote that few things catch a passing traveller's eye like the Drangur at Drangshlíð. Ninety-odd years of buses slowing down for the same stone, and it has not moved an inch.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🪨 Drangurinn
en: It later turned up as a location in the Viking film ***Hrafninn flýgur*** — "When the Raven Flies". Even the movies knew a dramatic rock when they saw one.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull
en: A gravel path pulls you toward **Sólheimajökull**, an outlet tongue of **Mýrdalsjökull** — Iceland's **fourth-largest ice cap**, and the lid on **Katla**. You are standing on the drainpipe of a buried volcano.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull
en: Up close the ice isn't white. It's streaked with **black ash bands** from **Katla** and **Eyjafjallajökull**, like a sooty paintbrush dragged across it. Each dark line is a bad year for somebody's washing.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull
en: In front sits a **blue-green lagoon** with small icebergs in it. The colour is **glacial flour** — rock ground so fine the water turns to liquid stone-dust. That lagoon is **new**. It is here because the ice is not.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull
en: Here is the part nobody makes up, because it is measured. **Somebody has walked out to this ice with a tape measure every year since 1930**, and the numbers are public. Over that whole record the front has pulled back **just under two kilometres — 1,995 metres.** Over the last ten years it has averaged **about 50 metres a year**; the most recent measured year, **2023 to 2024, was 43 metres.** The worst single year on record is **134 metres**, and it has happened **twice** — in **2007–08** and again in **2017–18**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull
en: And here is the bit that gets left out. **It is not a straight line down.** Between **1969 and 1995 this glacier ADVANCED in 23 years out of 29**, putting on **440 metres** — a quarter of a century of growing, in the middle of the record. That is why the measurements matter more than the slogan: real data has a reversal in it, and it still ends where this one ends.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull
en: Signs along the path mark where the front used to reach — "here… and here… and here." You have just walked **decades of retreat in a few minutes**, and the walk keeps getting longer.

en: From the bus you mostly see empty blackness. The real story is a crew that iced up over a glacier, glided to the coast, and **lived** — on a plane everyone insists on calling by the wrong name.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: Everyone calls it a "DC-3". It isn't. It is a **US Navy Super DC-3 — a Douglas R4D-8 / C-117D** — same family, the cousin who went to the gym. It has worn the wrong name for fifty years and has long since stopped correcting anybody.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: On **21 November 1973** it was flying **Höfn to Keflavík** when **ice choked both carburettors** over the **Vatnajökull** ice cap and both engines quit. The tourist version — that it "ran out of fuel" — is wrong. It iced up, and became, in the crew's own description, a massively overweight glider.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: The pilot turned **south for the coast** and put it down on the black sand. **All seven crew walked away.** The Navy stripped out the useful parts and left the bare hull sitting there, which is how you end up with an aeroplane as a landmark.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: For decades it was a quiet local curiosity. Then came a **Bieber video in 2015**, the Bollywood hit *Dilwale*, and Instagram, and that was that. **Cars were banned in 2016**, so now you walk a **4 km track each way** across old ocean floor in order to touch a plane with no wings.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: ⚠️ And that walk deserves respect. **Eight kilometres round trip across open sandur with no shelter of any kind** — not a tree, not a rock, not a wall — and no vehicle coming to get you. The weather out there can change while you are still walking out. It is a proper expedition dressed up as a photo stop.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: 🎬 **On screen:** a music-video magnet — **Justin Bieber's** "I'll Show You" (2015), Sigur Rós's *Heima* documentary (2007), and Bollywood's *Dilwale* ("Gerua") all used the plane and the black desert around it.

en: The Island That Got Left Behind

ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey
en: A **288-metre lump of frozen explosion** that used to be a real island — submarine volcano, sailors' landmark, and a cave with a chapel, a shieling and a monster in it. **Most mountains never have a CV that long.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey
en: **Pétursey** is **móberg** — the ash-and-rubble palagonite rock you get when a volcano **erupts under water or ice**. Hot magma met cold sea, shattered mid-blast, and cemented into these steep walls. Same recipe as nearby **Drangurinn**. **Landmælingar Íslands** puts the summit crags at **288 metres**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey
en: It was not always a mountain in a field. **Its old name was Háey — "the high island"** — and Iceland's national place-name record says so outright: *Pétursey var nefnd Háey eða Eyjan há í gömlum ritum.* The Atlantic really did go all the way round it, and sailors steered by it, until **Katla's black sand filled the gap and stranded it inland.** The island is still here. The sea moved out.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey
en: At the foot on the north side is **Eyjarhellir**, a cave big enough to echo, and the official place-name record for it reads like a short story. There are **ancient man-made marks** inside. Its side chamber is called **Stúkan** — the chapel stall — and was held to be **an old chapel**, until a landslide closed the door on it. **Loðmundur**, the settler at Sólheimar, is said to have kept his **shieling** in there. And the record ends by wondering whether **papar** — Irish monks, here before the Norse — lived in it, and whether the marks in Stúkan are theirs.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey
en: It also had a tenant nobody wanted. An **óvættur**, a malevolent thing, lived in Eyjarhellir and was seen before **blizzards and fatal accidents**. It was last seen around **1900**, in the shape of a dog that **grew until it was a troll reaching halfway up the mountain.** Horses refused to pass the cave mouth. A second-sighted farmer named **Indriði** reckoned the creature spent its time fighting the **water-demon of Klifandi** — and that this was the only reason Klifandi had not washed Pétursey's fields away. Which it has, partly, anyway. Even the monster was only doing an adequate job.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey
en: The name travelled. A line-fishing boat called **Pétursey** was lost in **March 1941** on passage to Scotland, and was reported sunk. This coast names its boats after its landmarks, and the war took some of them back.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey
en: The cliffs still work as a **seabird colony** — fulmars and **puffins** wheeling round it as though it never stopped being an island. Two farms sit at the base: **Eystri-** and **Vestri-Pétursey.**

en: If you squint, you can almost see Hallgrímskirkja **hiding inside** this little red-roofed church — it just needed a son with a big imagination and a state architect's salary.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja
en: This modest church was built by the master carpenter **Samúel Jónsson** — by all accounts a prolific and well-respected house-builder — one of those simple, sturdy rural churches put up to shrug off wind, rain and ash.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja
en: His son, **Guðjón Samúelsson**, was born **16 April 1887** and became **húsameistari ríkisins**, the state architect, **from 1915 until he died on 25 April 1950**. Thirty-five years designing the country. The University of Iceland made him an **honorary doctor of philosophy in June 1940**, which is not a thing that usually happens to carpenters' sons from Mýrdalur.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja
en: His **Hallgrímskirkja** — the basalt-column church on the Reykjavík hill — took **forty-one years to build** and was **consecrated in 1986**. Guðjón had been dead for **thirty-six** of those years. He drew the most recognisable building in Iceland and never saw it standing.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja
en: Look at this roof, then picture that one. You can feel these small rural churches — built plain, built to last, built for weather — echoing in the capital's skyline. Iceland's grandest church is a farm chapel that went to architecture school.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: **Dýrhólaey** means "door-hill island", and Iceland's own conservation service describes it precisely: a **120-metre móbergsstapi** — a tuff tuya — **formed in an eruption in the sea**, taking its name from the **arch rock** that from either side looks like an enormous doorway cut in a sheer cliff. Half of it is tuff, **Háey**; half is basalt, **Lágey**. And despite the *-ey*, the "island" on the end of its name, **it is firmly attached to the mainland.** It has been misnamed for a thousand years and nobody has bothered to fix it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: Sailors were less romantic. They called the hole **Portlandið** — or just **Húllið**, the hull.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: On top sits a castle-like lighthouse, one of the most powerful lights on this coast, **built in 1927**. It is there because this headland is the first thing a ship coming out of the Atlantic sees, and the last thing it wants to hit.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: From up there you can read the whole **Katla Corridor** in one turn of the head — the sandur behind, the **Reynisdrangar** needles ahead, and the Atlantic hurling itself at the basalt. It is a **seabird city**: Dýrhólaey has been a **friðland — a protected nature reserve — since 1978**, all **1.51 km²** of it, and the official reason is not the view, it is the **birds**. Parts close in the nesting season for the puffins, there is a **ranger here all year**, and the rules are the birds' rules.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: It was long called the **southernmost point of the mainland** — until **Katla's 1918 flood built Kötlutangi**, which took the title off it for several decades, before the sea carried that sand west again. The volcano moved the goalposts; the Atlantic moved them back.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: And in **October 1993**, pilot **Arngrímur Jóhannsson** and MP **Árni Johnsen** flew a light aircraft through the arch. *Morgunblaðið* ran it as "the first aeroplane through Dyrhólaey". Three passes — because if you only do it once, people will say you meant to miss.

en: 🎬 **On screen:** *Game of Thrones* used the beach below as **Eastwatch-by-the-Sea** (Season 7), and it has turned up in *Vikings* and *Beowulf & Grendel* as well.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar
en: One stop: black sand, columnar basalt, wave erosion, and a couple of trolls who lost track of the time — and a sea that has killed people. Awe first, feet planted well back.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar
en: Black sand. A basalt pipe-organ. Sea stacks offshore. **Iceland's most beautiful beach — and its most dangerous. Never turn your back on these waves.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar
en: ⚠️ **Before anything else.** The Icelandic word is **laumualda** — a "sneaking wave". It runs far higher up the beach than the sea in front of you suggests, the water is freezing, and the undertow pulls. **At least five people have been killed by this surf since 2007**, the most recent of them reported in June 2022; a **warning-light system** went up that same summer. Stay high on the dry sand, keep off the wet, and do not turn your back on the water for a photograph. The beach takes about **half a million visitors a year** and has no opinion about any of them.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar
en: Under your feet: fine **black volcanic sand** — basalt that met the sea, shattered, and got ground down to grains. **No shells, no coral, just pulverised volcano.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar
en: To one side, **Hálsanefshellir** — the shallow cave with its pipe-organ wall of **hexagonal columns** under the **Garðar** cliff. That is **stuðlaberg**: lava that cooled so slowly it contracted and cracked into near-perfect six-sided pillars. Same trick as the Giant's Causeway, better acoustics.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar
en: Out in the surf stand the **Reynisdrangar** sea stacks, the last hard bones of an old headland the sea otherwise chewed away — the "stack" at the end of the crack-cave-arch-stack sequence, and you can see every stage of it from where you stand.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar
en: In the legend they are **two night-trolls and a ship**, caught by the sunrise mid-theft and turned to stone. Icelandic trolls are strictly nocturnal; daylight is their kryptonite. They have been standing there mid-heist for a few thousand years, which is the longest anyone has ever been caught in the act.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar
en: Above, the **Reynisfjall** cliffs fill with nesting seabirds in summer — **puffins, fulmars and guillemots**. Bring the zoom as well as the wide angle.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: Under that ice sits **Katla**, and she is not a tidy cone. **Veðurstofa Íslands** puts the system at **about 80 km long**, reaching **around 1,500 m**, with an **ice-filled caldera** and fissure swarms running **northeast towards Síðujökull**. The caldera is not the neat ten-kilometre circle you will read online — that came from a proposed shape in a 1973 paper. The Icelandic geoscience journal **Jökull** describes something elongated, roughly **100 km²**. Either way: the mountain you cannot see is bigger than the mountains you can.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: The lid is **Mýrdalsjökull**, Iceland's **fourth-largest ice cap** — **520 km² when it was surveyed in 2019** — sitting on the furnace like several hundred metres of insulation. Being subglacial is the entire danger. She doesn't just throw ash; she **flash-melts a glacier into a flood.** Veðurstofa is blunt about it: without the ice on top, these would probably just be lava eruptions.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: She is the **fourth most active volcanic system in Iceland**, with **at least 21 eruptions in the last 1,100 years**. The last one to break through the ice was **1918**. From the settlement to 1918 the **average gap between eruptions was about 50 years**; Jökull's commonly cited range is **every 40 to 80**. It is now **108 years**. Do that sum on a bus and watch the faces change.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: An eruption under ice makes a **jökulhlaup**, and the estimates for Katla's peak discharge run to around **300,000 cubic metres a second** — an estimate, not a gauged reading, because nobody has ever stood downstream with a flow meter and lived to publish. Historically those floods came down **Mýrdalssandur**; in prehistory they also came down **Markarfljót**. The town of **Vík** has drilled for this for decades.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: **12 October 1918** is the date that rearranged the map. The flood carried so much sediment to the sea that it **pushed the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km** — a saga headland that once stood by open water is now stranded **inland**. A volcano that does land reclamation.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: Even asleep she exhales. A **2018 study in Geophysical Research Letters** — Ilyinskaya and colleagues, flying instruments over the ice in **2016 and 2017** — measured **12 to 24 kilotonnes of CO₂ a day** coming off Katla, which would make her one of the largest measured carbon sources among the world's *non-erupting* volcanoes, perhaps **4% of the global total**. Nobody has repeated the measurement since, so treat it as a photograph of two summers, not a live feed.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: And the family has a bigger member. The **Eldgjá** eruption, on the same system's fissure swarm, **began around 939 CE** and produced **about 20 km³ of lava and tephra** — Veðurstofa's own figure. For scale, the **Holuhraun eruption of 2014–15**, which most of us watched on the news, made about **1.5 km³**. Eldgjá was over thirteen times that.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / ⛪ Víkurkirkja
en: **Víkurkirkja** was consecrated on **Sunday 14 October 1934** — *Lesbók Morgunblaðsins* reported it that week — and Vík has been a church site ever since. It sits high on the hill for exactly one reason, and the reason is **Katla**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / ⛪ Víkurkirkja
en: If the volcano erupts under **Mýrdalsjökull**, the **jökulhlaup** comes down **Mýrdalssandur**, the way Veðurstofa says it has come in historical times, and it could take the whole village with it. This church stands on the **only ground high enough** to be above the water.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / ⛪ Víkurkirkja
en: Every resident is trained to **run to this church** the moment the sirens sound. Not to gather belongings, not to fetch the car — run, uphill, now. In Vík, "run to church" is not a sermon. It is disaster policy with a steeple on it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / ⛪ Víkurkirkja
en: Which makes it the only building in Iceland where the architecture and the emergency plan are the same object.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal
en: Vík is Iceland's **southernmost mainland village**, strung along the beach with **Víkurkirkja** parked safely up on the hill — the official *run here if Katla wakes* point. There is **no natural harbour** anywhere along this coast, so historically this was a place you **rowed boats out through the surf from an open shore.** Yes. On purpose. For fish.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal
en: It is not the sleepy outpost it used to be. **740 people in the village and 1,004 in Mýrdalshreppur on 1 January 2026** — and the district was **451 in 2012**. It has **more than doubled in fourteen years**, which for an Icelandic village is a population explosion conducted entirely by tour bus.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal
en: Here is a thing worth getting right, because you will hear both numbers. Vík is, in **Veðurstofa's own wording, the warmest weather station in the country *ásamt Vestmannaeyjakaupstað*** — "along with Vestmannaeyjar". Over the standard period **1971–2000 its annual mean is 5.3 °C**. Over the station's **last two decades, 1991–2013, it is 5.9 °C**. Both figures are real; they are simply different slices of time, and the gap between them is the warming. Reykjavík did the same thing over the same window, **4.3 °C up to 5.1 °C**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal
en: "Warmest" is doing heroic work in that sentence, by the way. The warmest year in Vík's entire record is **6.7 °C, in 2003**, the coldest is **4.1 °C in 1979**, and the lowest temperature ever logged there is **−16.9 °C on 1 April 1968** — an April Fool's joke delivered with a thermometer.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal
en: It is also properly, professionally wet: **2,317 mm a year across 1971–2000**, against Reykjavík's **822 mm**. That is **2.8 times** the capital's rainfall, and Vík's own wettest year was **2,973 mm in 2007**. Still not the champion — **Kvísker**, out east under Öræfajökull, averages **3,457 mm** and took **4,630.4 mm in 2002**, with **293.3 mm falling in a single January day**. When Kvísker has a wet year, it does not do it quietly.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal
en: In **1918 Katla** erupted under the ice and sent a **jökulhlaup** to the sea so vast it **pushed the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km**, burying everything under fresh sand. **Hjörleifshöfði** — a saga headland that once stood by open sea — is now stranded **inland**, the gap quietly filled by a century of Katla's black homework.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal
en: 🎬 **On screen:** the mountains right behind town played **Siberia** in *Captain America: Civil War* (2016), and Vík is the whole backdrop for Netflix's Icelandic series *Katla* (2021). A village that gets cast as Siberia has made peace with its weather.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: Most countries' founding stories are statues and speeches. Iceland's is a body, a fake bear, and a woman who became a volcano.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: That massive rock is a **1,100-year-old crime scene** — and the address of Iceland's most famous ghost.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: **Hjörleifshöfði** is a **222-metre móberg headland** — Landmælingar Íslands' own survey figure — named for **Hjörleifur Hróðmarsson**, sworn **blood-brother of Ingólfur Arnarson, Iceland's first settler**. The two sailed here together around **874** and then split. Ingólfur let the gods choose, following his high-seat pillars to Reykjavík. Hjörleifur, who **refused to sacrifice to any god at all**, parked at the first headland he came to. **His burial mound still crowns the summit.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: Come the spring, says *Landnámabók*, he had **one ox** — so he had his **enslaved Irishmen drag the plough** instead. They killed the ox and **blamed a bear**. Iceland **has no bears.** The newcomers simply did not know that yet, and when they scattered across the sand to hunt an animal that does not exist here, the thralls **ambushed them one by one**, Hjörleifur included, and fled with the women and the boats to the islands offshore.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: Ingólfur found the bodies, tracked the killers out to those islands and killed every one of them. *Landnámabók* has him stand over his blood-brother and say, in effect, that it is a sad end for a good man to die at the hands of slaves — and that this is what comes of refusing to sacrifice. Even the eulogy is a told-you-so.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: And the islands kept the name. They are the **Vestmannaeyjar**, the **"Isles of the West Men"** — *vestmenn* being the Norse word for the **Gaels of Ireland and the Hebrides**. The archipelago out there is **named after the enslaved men who did the killing.** The postcard version of free, self-made Viking farmers is missing a chapter.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: The ghost arrives **three centuries later**. **Katla**, a fearsome housekeeper at the nearby monastery of **Þykkvabæjarklaustur**, owned **a pair of breeches that never tired**. The shepherd **Barði** borrowed them; she **drowned him in the whey vat**. As the whey sank and the body came closer to showing, she walked out onto **Mýrdalsjökull** and threw herself into the chasm still called **Kötlugjá — "Katla's rift"**. Soon afterwards a **flood burst out of the ice**. **The volcano is named after her**, and every eruption since has been blamed on her temper.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: Like Pétursey back down the road, this cape **was once an island** — now tethered to Iceland by miles of Katla's black sand. At its foot sits **Kötluklettur**, "Katla's Rock", in case anyone was in danger of forgetting whose neighbourhood this is.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: 🎬 **On screen:** this headland and the black sand around it became the planet **Lah'mu**, Jyn Erso's childhood home, in *Rogue One* (2016). The famous "Yoda Cave" — **Gígjagjá** — is cut into this very massif.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss
en: The **Skógá** river skips the rapids and walks straight off the old sea-cliff — **about 60 metres down and 25 metres wide** — free-falling into a deep pool before racing across the sandur to the Atlantic. At the base you have to **shout to be heard**, which is why most videos from here are people silently pointing at it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss
en: This cliff is the **coastline of thousands of years ago**, and it is textbook waterfall geology: hard cap-rock over soft, undercut until it collapses, so the fall eats its way **upstream** and leaves a gorge behind it. Then the land lifted, the rivers dumped black sand, and the real shore marched several kilometres south. **Skógafoss never moved. The sea did.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss
en: The metal staircase on the right is your free fitness test. At the top begins the **Fimmvörðuháls** trail, which climbs between **Eyjafjallajökull and Mýrdalsjökull** — the same gap the 2010 eruption cracked open to start with.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss
en: And there is treasure in it. **Landnámabók** names **Þrasi Þórólfsson inn gamli** as the settler at Skógar — folklore shifts him a little east to Þrasastaðir, so even his address is disputed — and the story says he hid a **chest of gold behind the falls**. Someone eventually got a hand to it, hooked the **iron ring** on the chest, and pulled. The ring came off. The chest did not. That is the whole legend and it is, frankly, the most Icelandic ending available.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss
en: Behind the car park sits **Skógar Museum** — turf houses, an old church, farm buildings, assembled over a lifetime by **Þórður Tómasson** — and one gorge along, a bonus waterfall called **Kvernufoss** that almost every coach drives straight past.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss
en: 🎬 **On screen:** the big one for filmmakers — *Thor: The Dark World* (2013), *Vikings* (Floki's storyline, Season 5), a *Game of Thrones* aerial sequence in the final season, the old *Beowulf & Grendel* (2005), India's *Dilwale*, *Aadhavan* and *Namo Venkatesa* — and yes, **Justin Bieber** clambered up it for "I'll Show You".

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Seljalandsfoss / 💧 Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi
en: **Seljalandsfoss** drops off Iceland's old sea-cliff, fed by the **Seljalandsá** running down off **Eyjafjallajökull**. *Morgunblaðið* puts it at **62 metres**; you will also see 60 quoted. What nobody mentions is that it is the **first and lowest fall on the river** — there are more of them upstream, and not one coach stops for any of them.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Seljalandsfoss / 💧 Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi
en: A natural recess lets you walk **all the way behind the curtain** in summer. Wet, slippery rock, so: good boots, a waterproof, and **one hand free**. In ice the path closes, and the barrier means it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Seljalandsfoss / 💧 Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi
en: The cliff itself is an **old sea cliff from just after the Ice Age**, when the Atlantic came right to the foot of the **Eyjafjöll**. Rivers then filled the lowlands and the coast is now several kilometres south — the same drowned-then-stranded shoreline as Skógafoss down the road. **The sea left. The waterfalls stayed.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Seljalandsfoss / 💧 Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi
en: A short walk north, **Gljúfrabúi** — "the canyon-dweller" — hides in a narrow mossy gorge with only its top showing. It is on a different river: the **Gljúfurá**, also called **Hamragarðaá**, which runs down beside the Seljalandsá. To meet it you **wade up the stream**, and **wet feet are non-negotiable**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Seljalandsfoss / 💧 Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / ⛪ Hofskirkja
en: Everything you will ever read says this church was built in **1884.** Both the bodies that actually own and protect it — **Þjóðminjasafn Íslands** and **Minjastofnun** — say the build ran **1883 to 1885.** The joiner was **Páll Pálsson** from **Hörgsdalur.** So it is not a Viking church, it is Victorian, and it is younger than the Eiffel Tower.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / ⛪ Hofskirkja
en: Look at how it is put together, because it is three different buildings at once: a **timber frame** inside, **long walls of stacked stone with no mortar**, and a roof of **stone slabs with turf laid over the top.** Most turf buildings are turf walls. This one is drystone under a stone roof — which is the rare bit.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / ⛪ Hofskirkja

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / ⛪ Hofskirkja

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / ⛪ Hofskirkja

ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / 🧭 Ingólfshöfði
en: Iceland's founding year — **874** — is **not written down anywhere.** It is a **sum.** Somebody did the arithmetic centuries later, and we have been printing the answer ever since.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / 🧭 Ingólfshöfði
en: Out there is **Ingólfshöfði.** **Landnámabók** says Ingólfur made landfall at the headland that now carries his name. Read the actual text and it is subtler than the postcard: the phrase is **"annan vetur" — a second winter** — and it comes *after* the business with his blood-brother Hjörleifur, not before it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / 🧭 Ingólfshöfði
en: **874 comes from a calculation in Landnáma's prologue**, pinning the voyage to the reign of Haraldur hárfagri. **Íslendingabók** — written by **Ari fróði**, and the older book of the two — points at roughly **870** instead. The neat date is later arithmetic, not a record.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / 🧭 Ingólfshöfði
en: The **Vísindavefur** at the University of Iceland puts it plainly: Ingólfur is "first settler" **by convention.** **Hrafna-Flóki**, **Garðar Svavarsson** and **Náttfari** are all in the same sources, all here earlier. He got the title because his descendants ran the parliament and wrote the book.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / 🧭 Ingólfshöfði
en: The headland itself: **76 metres** high, **1,200 by 750 metres**, cliffs on every side but the west. It is **basalt lava sitting on a base of hyaloclastite** — hard cap, soft footing, which is why the sea has not taken it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / 🧭 Ingólfshöfði
en: **It used to be an island.** The glacial rivers filled the gap with sand and joined it onto Iceland. The ground you are crossing built the bridge.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fjallsárlón → Jökulsárlón - 10 minutes drive folks / Breiðamerkursandur

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið
en: **Road 56 — Vatnaleið**, "the lakes route" — is very nearly the newest thing you will touch all day, and the Road Administration wrote the date down. **Friday 2 November 2001**: the transport minister **Sturla Böðvarsson** cut the ribbon, helped by the director of roads, **Helgi Hallgrímsson**. That same day the old **Kerlingarskarð** pass was retired after generations of hauling traffic over the peninsula's spine.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið
en: It was not a foregone conclusion either. ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið
en: The numbers are the point of it: **16.4 km** of new road topping out at **230 m**, against Kerlingarskarð's **311 m** — and only **3 km** of it above 200 metres, where the old road had **ten**. **We replaced the pass, not the mountains.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið
en: Those flat-topped mountains flanking the road are **móberg** — the fought-a-glacier-and-lost rock, now on both sides of you. The whole spine of Snæfellsnes is built of it, and the ice sheet that made it left ten thousand years ago and never came back for its work.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið
en: **Baulárvallavatn** sits just west of the road, one of the lakes that gave the route its name. And down in the bogs at the south end of **Sátudalur**, two streams rise almost side by side and then immediately fall out with each other: **Rauðusteinalækur** runs south into Baulárvallavatn and eventually reaches the sea as Straumfjarðará, while **Fossá** runs north. Same bog, opposite coasts.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar
en: Iceland's most famous islands are named after ten murdered Irishmen. Nobody puts that on the postcard.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar
en: It begins with a wedding threat. Ingólfur and his sworn brother **Leifur** went raiding with the three sons of **Atli jarl hinn mjóvi** of Gaular, and at the feast **Hólmsteinn** announced he would marry **Helga Arnardóttir** — *“eða öngva konu ella”*, **or no woman at all.** Helga was **Ingólfur's sister and Leifur's wife.** (You can see where this is heading.) **Two of the three brothers died** in the fighting, the pair **forfeited their lands**, and they sailed for Iceland not as pioneers but as men with nothing left.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar
en: Leifur earned his nickname the hard way. Raiding in Ireland he broke into an underground chamber, found a man holding a sword in the dark and killed him for it — *“síðan var hann kallaður Hjörleifur.”* **Sword-Leifur** (*hjör* is sword). On that same raid he took **ten slaves**, five of them named: **Dufþakur**, Geirröður, Skjaldbjörn, Halldór and Drafdittur. **He picked up his name and his killers off the same beach.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar
en: Then the ox. They made land the same season and wintered apart — Ingólfur east at **Ingólfshöfði**, Hjörleifur at the headland on the south coast — and come spring he wanted to sow: *“hann átti einn uxa”*, **he had one ox** and ten men to pull against it. Dufþakur's plan was clean. **Kill the ox, blame a forest bear**, and take the Norsemen one at a time as they scatter to hunt an animal that does not exist in Iceland. *“Þá settu þrælarnir að sérhverjum þeirra og myrtu þá alla.”*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar
en: Ingólfur came west — *“Eftir það fór Ingólfur vestur til Hjörleifshöfða”* — stood over the body, and blamed **the gods**: *“Lítið lagðist hér fyrir góðan dreng, er þrælar skyldu að bana verða, og sé eg svo hverjum verða, ef eigi vill blóta”* — **little came to this brave man, that slaves should be his death, and so I see it goes for every man who will not sacrifice.** Ten enslaved men, one ox, and his conclusion was **insufficient piety.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar
en: He found them at **Eið** — *“Fundu þá þar sem Eið heitir í eyjunum”* — and they were **eating.** That is the low sand neck between **Heimaklettur** and **Stóra-Klif**, and the islanders have their own name for it: **Þrælaeiði, the Slaves' Isthmus.** Heimaslóð is blunt about why — *“þrælar Hjörleifs hafi komið þar að landi, og einhverjir þeirra líklega drepnir þar af Ingólfi Arnarsyni.”* **Ten men murdered their owner, rowed open ocean, made land — and stopped for a meal.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar
en: *“Ingólfur drap þá alla.”* **He killed them all.** **Dufþakur** went off the cliff at the place still called **Dufþaksskor**, on the north face of **Heimaklettur** — the **279-metre** mountain we sail underneath on the way into the harbour.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar
en: Then the sentence that names the map: *“Vestmannaeyjar heita þar síðan, er þrælarnir voru drepnir, því að þeir voru Vestmenn”* — the islands have been called Vestmannaeyjar ever since, **because the slaves were West Men.** Irish and Hebridean Gaels. What is out there today: **14 to 18 islands**, depending on how small a rock you are willing to promote, plus about **30 skerries and sea stacks** — and only **Heimaey** is inhabited, **4,518 people** as of **1 January 2026**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Mainland → Landeyjahöfn / 🏝️ Vestmannaeyjar
en: And here is the one thing I cannot give you: **a year.** **Landnámabók puts no date on any of it** — not the killing, not the pursuit, not the naming — and the book was written **roughly three hundred years after the events**, in the twelfth century, about the ninth. Vísindavefurinn's own historian **Helgi Þorláksson** rejects the literary Ingólfur outright and calls it *“samkomulagsatriði”*, **a matter of agreement**, that the first settler lived in Reykjavík and was called Ingólfur. The one firm date came out of a volcano: *“menn voru á ferð í Reykjavík þegar fyrir 871 ± 2”* — people were already moving about Reykjavík before **871, plus or minus two.** That is the **landnámslag**, the settlement ash layer, dated against ice cores. **The saga gives me names, numbers and a meal. The only thing it will not give me is a year — and for that I have to ask a volcano.**
